claims_disputed.claim: Dependency-aware parallel execution improves execution efficiency.
claims_disputed.reason: Nothing isolates parallel execution: there is no ATG-without-parallelism ablation, and Table 2 has one unlabelled row per method. ATG's lower step count is equally explained by fewer invalid actions (Table 3: 12% vs 43% of trajectories), and in single-agent stateful ALFWorld/WebShop the 'parallel' branches cannot run concurrently. Compile, check and repair LLM calls are excluded from the count.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: Same checkpoint, decoding config and action budget (§5.1): ATG beats ReAct/Reflexion in 9/9 backbone-benchmark cells, and so does PoG, a second LLM-DAG planner. Nothing in the paper points the other way; the only loss is to GPT-4 ReAct, a cross-model comparison. The weak, uncompute-matched, unreleased evidence is already captured by claim strength (all weak). 'mixed' would count this paper toward 'contested' without any contrary data.
Same evidence as P37 (recursive decomposition then execution vs flat same-model loops); the review itself says 'same caveats as P37'. Direction is uniformly positive, strength weak.

missed_issues: The PoG baseline is itself an LLM-generated parallel DAG planner, and it beats ReAct and Reflexion in all 9 cells (e.g. Mistral ALFWorld 23.72 vs 6.57). That is a second same-model DAG-vs-loop result. It also shows the DAG alone is not what gives ATG its 20-50 point lead over PoG.

ATG scores are nearly backbone-invariant (ALFWorld 55.7/58.7/63.7; WebShop 62.8/64.9/68.4) while every baseline swings widely across backbones (Gemma WebShop: ReAct 5.93, PoG 12.56). The per-environment 'atomic tool' set (Definition 2 allows task-specific functions) is never listed, so ATG may get higher-level actions or task-specific prompts that the baselines lack.
Fig. 6 reports 'failure precision' >74% and 'repair success rate' with no stated ground truth for a 'risky plan' and no sample size.
Test-set sizes are never stated for any benchmark.
note: I agree with admit_with_caveats at low weight. I credit the stance more than the review did: two different LLM-DAG planners beat same-model linear loops everywhere, so the direction is clear for 7-8B models in text environments. I discount the magnitude more: the ATG numbers barely depend on the backbone, the tools and prompts are unreleased, and no claim exceeds weak. Nothing here bears on frontier-model coding agents.
